implementation_notes: The classic structure as an API: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) is the worker set (threads reused, tasks queued on its unbounded work queue), submit() of Callables returns Futures, and ExecutorCompletionService places each finished task on a completion queue so the master consumes results in completion order with take() rather than in submission order. It is the default when the master must stream partial results or react to the fastest task; the pool must be shut down explicitly.
pitfalls: A bounded pool plus futures that block waiting on other futures deadlocks; completion-order collection must not depend on a result that is still queued.
The executor's work queue is unbounded: submitting a huge task list queues everything in memory before the first result appears.
Futures are not collected automatically: without take()/get() on every submitted task, worker failures vanish.

variants.name: Fixed thread pool + ExecutorCompletionService (Java 8)

variants.name: CompletableFuture.supplyAsync + allOf composition
variants.implementation_notes: The fan-out expressed as composition: each subtask is a CompletableFuture running on a supplied Executor, and the master combines the partials with allOf/thenCombine or a reduction over the futures - no blocking until the final join. One failed subtask completes the derived future exceptionally while the siblings keep running, so failure policy (fail fast versus collect and decide) must be stated; use it when the aggregation itself is further composed into a larger asynchronous pipeline.
pitfalls: Without an explicit Executor, supplyAsync uses the common ForkJoinPool, which is shared with every parallel stream in the JVM.
join() wraps failures in CompletionException and tells nothing about which subtask failed; attach per-future handling if the aggregate must report causes.
Composing futures that depend on each other reintroduces ordering; the fan-out stays independent only if the partial results are.

variants.name: Virtual threads per task (Java 21)
variants.implementation_notes: Java 21 makes the worker pool cheap enough to stop pooling: newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor creates one virtual thread per subtask, so blocking I/O no longer needs a sized pool and the master's concurrency limit becomes a policy decision (semaphores or StructuredTaskScope) rather than a resource bound. Choose it for I/O-bound fan-out; for CPU-bound work the useful parallelism is still the number of carrier threads, so a fixed platform-thread pool remains the right shape.
pitfalls: Virtual threads do not bypass CPU limits: CPU-bound subtasks still serialise on the carrier pool, so unbounded virtual threads just queue.
Pinning (a synchronized block around a blocking call, or a native frame) can block a carrier thread and stall unrelated virtual threads.
Per-task virtual threads make the failure surface larger: use StructuredTaskScope or explicit exception handling to keep the aggregate's semantics.
